# Brief: digitise the photographic archive, and decide what "digitised" means

The archive is about forty thousand items in eleven filing cabinets, plus an
unknown quantity in the two crates that came from the old office and have never
been opened. We have funding for one year of one person plus equipment. That is
not enough to do everything properly, so the first real deliverable of this
project is a decision about what we are actually doing.

## The material

Mostly prints, mostly monochrome, mostly between forty and eighty years old.
Perhaps a fifth are negatives, in sleeves, in no order that anybody has been able
to establish. A small number of glass plates in the bottom drawer of cabinet
nine, which nobody has touched in living memory and which should probably be
handled by somebody who knows what they are doing rather than by us.

Condition ranges from fine to actively deteriorating. There is a smell from
cabinet four that suggests something in there is decomposing and that cabinet
should be assessed before anything else, on the grounds that it is the one where
delay costs material.

Cataloguing is partial and inconsistent. Roughly half the items have a written
caption on the reverse, in several hands, of varying reliability. There is an
index card system covering perhaps a third, which does not obviously correspond
to the current physical arrangement.

## The decision to make first

There are three defensible projects here and we can afford one:

- Scan everything at a modest resolution, catalogue minimally, and produce a
  browsable archive of forty thousand mediocre images with thin metadata. Fast,
  complete, and of limited scholarly value.
- Scan a selected subset at high resolution with proper cataloguing, and leave
  the rest in the cabinets. Valuable for what it covers, and it leaves the
  deterioration problem untouched for everything it does not.
- Prioritise by condition: assess everything, stabilise and scan what is at
  risk, catalogue as you go, and accept that the healthy material waits for a
  future project.

I lean towards the third and I hold that lightly. Make the case for whichever
you think is right, and make it in the first month, because the equipment
purchase depends on it and the equipment for the first option is not the
equipment for the second.

## Constraints

- Nothing leaves the building. The insurance position on the collection is
  unclear and until it is clarified the material stays here.
- Storage for the output has to be somewhere we will still be able to read in
  twenty years. That means an open format, a documented layout, and at least one
  copy somewhere that is not this building.
- The reading room stays open. It is used perhaps twice a month, and those two
  visits are the entire public face of the collection, so a project that makes
  the material unavailable for a year has damaged the thing it is meant to serve.

## What I want in the first month

- Cabinet four assessed, and whatever is decomposing dealt with.
- A condition survey good enough to support the decision above. Not item by
  item — a sample per drawer, extrapolated, with the method stated.
- The three options costed, in equipment and in time, with your recommendation.
- A note on the glass plates and the two crates, saying what expertise we need
  to bring in and roughly what it costs.

After that we will agree the shape and you can get on with it.

## A warning about scope

Every archive project I have seen has been eaten by cataloguing. Cataloguing is
the part that feels like real work, it is genuinely valuable, and it is
unbounded — there is always a better description to write, an attribution to
chase, a date to narrow down. A year disappears into the first two cabinets and
the other nine are exactly as they were.

Set a per-item time budget for cataloguing at the start, hold to it, and record
what you would have wanted to add so that a future project can pick it up. An
item with a thin record and a good scan is recoverable. An item still in the
cabinet is not.

## Reporting

Monthly, one page, to me. Include the count, because the count is what the
funder will ask about, and include one item you found interesting, because that
is what keeps anybody reading a monthly report.
